TargetRLF1: Sexually transmitted infections (STIs), also known as sexually transmitted diseases (STDs), are infections that are typically spread through sexual contact, including vaginal, anal, or oral sex. These infections can be caused by bacteria, viruses, or parasites, and they can have serious health consequences if left untreated. Common STIs include chlamydia, gonorrhoea, syphilis, genital herpes, human papillomavirus (HPV), and HIV/AIDS ayo Here are some ways to prevent the transmission of STIs:  Abstinence: The most effective way to prevent STIs is to abstain from sexual activity (vaginal, anal, or oral) with a partner who has an STI or whose STI status is unknown.  Use Condoms: Consistently and correctly using condoms during sexual activity can significantly reduce the risk of STI transmission. Use latex or polyurethane condoms for vaginal or anal sex, and use condoms or dental dams for oral sex.  Limit Sexual Partners: Having fewer sexual partners reduces your risk of exposure to STIs. Mutual monogamy with a partner who has tested negative for STIs can also lower your risk.  Communication: Talk openly and honestly with your sexual partners about STIs, testing, and safer sex practices. Encourage each other to get tested regularly for STIs.  Get Tested: Get tested for STIs regularly, especially if you are sexually active with multiple partners or have had unprotected sex. Many STIs do not cause symptoms, so testing is the only way to know your STI status.  Vaccination: Vaccines are available to prevent certain STIs, such as HPV and hepatitis B. Talk to your healthcare provider about whether vaccination is appropriate for you.  Avoid Sharing Needles: If you use injectable drugs, never share needles or other drug paraphernalia. Sharing needles can transmit STIs such as HIV and hepatitis B and C.  Practice Safer Sex: Avoid high-risk sexual behaviors, such as unprotected sex with multiple partners or engaging in sex while under the influence of drugs or alcohol. Use your best judgment and prioritize your health and safety.  Routine Health Care: Attend regular check-ups with your healthcare provider for sexual health screenings and preventive care. Seek medical attention promptly if you experience symptoms of an STI or have been exposed to an STI.  By practicing safer sex, getting tested regularly, and communicating openly with your sexual partners, you can reduce your risk of contracting STIs and protect your sexual health. If you have questions or concerns about STI prevention, don't hesitate to speak with a healthcare provider or sexual health professional for guidance and support.

TargetRLF1: A chlamydia also known as Chlamydial Genitourinary infection test detects the bacteria that cause chlamydia, a sexually transmitted infection (STI). This test tells you if you have the chlamydia infection so that you can get treat treatment and avoid complications. Your provider takes a sample of urine or secretions from your vagina, penis or rectum and sends it to a lab for testing using a test called NAATs (short for nucleic acid amplification tests), which is very accurate and easy to take. Results are usually ready in a day. Less often, providers use a cell culture to test for chlamydia. In this case, your provider swabs your vagina, urethra or anus to collect a sample of fluid and cells. They send the cells to a lab to test. If bacteria are present, they will grow, which indicates an infection. Providers may choose this type of chlamydia test to detect infections in the anus. Or they may use a cell culture to see how chlamydia treatments are working. Because of the possibility of multiple sexually transmitted infections, all patients with any sexually transmitted disease (STD) should be evaluated for chlamydial infection. There are no risks involved with these tests. Rarely the results of the tests may be inconclusive or unclear and you may need to give another sample.

This test tells you if you have the chlamydia infection so that you can get treat treatment and avoid complications.. You should get tested regularly if you have unprotected sex with a new partner, multiple partners or a partner who has an STI. You should also get tested if you have symptoms or you are pregnant. Many people with Chlamydia don't have symptoms. Because of the possibility of multiple sexually transmitted infections, all patients with any sexually transmitted disease (STD) should be evaluated for chlamydial infection.

TargetRLF1: While some people with Genital Herpes or Herpes Simplex Virus (HSV), also known as herpes will never have any symptoms, other people can develop symptoms within a few weeks of being infected. Common oral herpes symptoms include blisters (cold sores) or open sores (ulcers) in or around the mouth or lips. Most people notice a group or cluster of blisters or ulcers (lesions). These lesions burn and can be painful. They can appear on the buttocks, anus or thighs, on the vulva or vagina in women, and on the penis or scrotum in men. Often, before the lesions appear, patients describe a prodrome, characterized by a tingling or burning sensation in the area where the lesions will develop that can be noticed during urination, along with itching or discomfort in the genital area. You can also have the following symptoms, Blisters on the mouth or lips, Fever, headache or pain in the joints, Trouble urinating. In case of Neonatal Herpes, signs that your baby may have herpes are:irritability, blisters anywhere on her body, trouble breathing, grunting, blue appearance (cyanosis), rapid breathing, short periods of no breathing, jaundice, bleeding easily. People can have repeated outbreaks over time (‘recurrences’). These are usually shorter and less severe than the first outbreak. Herpes is a lifelong sexually transmitted infection, that cannot be cured. However, the number of outbreaks/recurrences may reduce over time.

TargetRLF1: A Urinary Tract Infection (UTI) and a Sexually Transmitted Infection (STI) are not the same.  A STI is an infection that is spread from one person to another through sexual intercourse. A UTI is infection of the bladder the kidney or the tubes connected to them. Bacteria that live in the genital and anal areas may move to the urinary tract and cause a UTI. Sexual intercourse can increase risk of getting a UTI if sexual activity introduces germs into your urinary tract but UTIs cannot be spread from one person to another. UTIs and STIs can also have similar symptoms such as fever, lower abdominal pain and pain on urination. Your healthworker will be able to do some tests to diffferentiate the two. A simple way to reduce your chances of getting a UTI is to urinate right after intercourse.

TargetRLF1: Gonorrhea may affect women and men differently. In women, it may show little to no symptoms for long periods of time. For men, two to five days after infection, they may experience pain or burning on urination, white or yellow discharge from penis and swollen testes. In women, symptoms can be subtle and may include pain or burning on urination, vaginal discharge and vaginal bleeding between periods and during intercourse. If the infection is in the throat it may cause redness, pain and a sore feeling, similar to a sore throat. Anal infections can cause discharge, bleeding, itchiness, soreness and painful bowel movements. In babies, eye infection can cause redness, pain, soreness, wounds in the eye, tearing, swollen eyelids and pus discharge, which can lead to blindness if untreated. If the gonorrhea infection is spread throughout the body, it can lead to joint pain, skin lesions, fever, and heart and brain complications.

Over the decades, the disease has spread all over the world.

Over the decades, the disease has spread all over the world.

TargetRLF1: A chlamydia also known as Chlamydial Genitourinary infection test detects the bacteria that cause chlamydia, a sexually transmitted infection (STI). This test tells you if you have the chlamydia infection so that you can get treat treatment and avoid complications. If bacteria are present, they will grow, which indicates an infection. Providers may choose this type of chlamydia test to detect infections in the anus. Or they may use a cell culture to see how chlamydia treatments are working. Because of the possibility of multiple sexually transmitted infections, all patients with any sexually transmitted disease (STD) should be evaluated for chlamydial infection. There are no risks involved with these tests. Rarely the results of the tests may be inconclusive or unclear and you may need to give another sample.

Over the decades, the disease has spread all over the world.

Because of the possibility of multiple sexually transmitted infections, all patients with any sexually transmitted disease (STD) should be evaluated for chlamydial infection. TargetRLF1: Human immunodeficiency virus is a zoonosis – an infection that originated in animals and passed into human hosts. It is closely related to the simian immunodeficiency virus (SIV) found in chimpanzees in central Africa. To date, the earliest known case of HIV-1 infection in human blood is from a sample taken in 1959 from a man who'd died in Kinshasa in what was then the Belgian Congo. SIV probably entered the human population as a result of hunting chimpanzees. It is plausible that transmission could have occurred through a hunter being wounded and blood from a chimpanzee entering his bloodstream. Chimpanzees avoid humans wherever possible, so it is likely that SIVcpz crossed into humans as a result of human encroachment into forest areas. The origin of the Human Immunodeficiency Virus (HIV) has been a subject of scientific research and debate since the virus was identified in the 1980s. It came to global attention after doctors started receiving reports of rare cases of pneumonia, cancer and other illnesses in young gay homosexual men and injection drug users. Over the decades, the disease has spread all over the world.

TargetRLF1: The only way to completely avoid STIs is to not have vaginal, anal, or oral sex. If you are sexually active, you can do the following things to lower your chances of getting Genital Herpes or Herpes Simplex Virus (HSV), also known as herpes:•        Being in a long-term mutually monogamous relationship with a partner who does not have herpes.•        Using condoms the right way every time you have sex.Be aware that not all herpes sores occur in areas that a condom can cover. Also, the skin can release the virus (shed) from areas that do not have a visible herpes sore. For these reasons, condoms may not fully protect you from getting herpes. If your sex partner(s) has/have genital herpes, you can lower your risk of getting it if:•        Your partner takes an anti-herpes medicine every day. This is something your partner should discuss with his or her healthcare provider.•        You avoid having vaginal, anal, or oral sex when your partner has herpes symptoms (i.e., during an "outbreak").If you are pregnant and have genital herpes, prenatal care visits are very important. Some research suggest that a genital herpes infection may lead to miscarriage or make it more likely to deliver your baby too early. You can pass herpes to your unborn child before birth, but it more commonly passes during delivery. This can lead to a deadly infection in your baby (called neonatal herpes). It is important that you avoid getting genital herpes during pregnancy. Tell your healthcare provider if you have ever had a genital herpes diagnosis or symptoms. Also tell them about any possible exposure to genital herpes. If you have genital herpes, you may need to take anti-herpes medicine towards the end of your pregnancy. This medicine may reduce your risk of having signs or symptoms of genital herpes when you deliver. At the time of delivery, your healthcare provider should carefully examine you for herpes sores. If you have signs or symptoms of genital herpes at delivery, a 'C-section' is likely to occur.

These are usually shorter and less severe than the first outbreak. Herpes is a lifelong sexually transmitted infection, that cannot be cured. However, the number of outbreaks/recurrences may reduce over time.

Also tell them about any possible exposure to genital herpes. If you have genital herpes, you may need to take anti-herpes medicine towards the end of your pregnancy. If you have signs or symptoms of genital herpes at delivery, a 'C-section' is likely to occur.

TargetRLF1: Uncomplicated Chlamydia also known as Chlamydial Genitourinary infection can be easily cured with antibiotics and is usually resolved within days or weeks. It is important that you take all of the medicine your healthcare provider gives you because untreated or improperly treated Chlamydia can lead to serious complications. Do not share medicine for chlamydia with anyone. Recommended drugs include Doxycylcine, Azithromycin, Levofloxacin and Amoxicillin. When taken properly, drugs will stop the infection and could decrease your chances of having problems later. Although medicine will stop the infection, it will not undo any permanent damage caused by the disease. You should notify your sexual partner(s) to get tested and treated, if necessary. Repeat infection with chlamydia is common. You should receive testing again about three months after your treatment, even if your sex partner(s) receives treatment. If the mother had a documented chlamydial infection during pregnancy that was untreated, presumptively treat the infant, even without confirmation of infection.

TargetRLF1: While some people with Genital Herpes or Herpes Simplex Virus (HSV), also known as herpes will never have any symptoms, other people can develop symptoms within a few weeks of being infected. Common oral herpes symptoms include blisters (cold sores) or open sores (ulcers) in or around the mouth or lips. Most people notice a group or cluster of blisters or ulcers (lesions). These lesions burn and can be painful. They can appear on the buttocks, anus or thighs, on the vulva or vagina in women, and on the penis or scrotum in men. Often, before the lesions appear, patients describe a prodrome, characterized by a tingling or burning sensation in the area where the lesions will develop that can be noticed during urination, along with itching or discomfort in the genital area. You can also have the following symptoms, Blisters on the mouth or lips, Fever, headache or pain in the joints, Trouble urinating. In case of Neonatal Herpes, signs that your baby may have herpes are:irritability, blisters anywhere on her body, trouble breathing, grunting, blue appearance (cyanosis), rapid breathing, short periods of no breathing, jaundice, bleeding easily. People can have repeated outbreaks over time (‘recurrences’). These are usually shorter and less severe than the first outbreak. Herpes is a lifelong sexually transmitted infection, that cannot be cured. However, the number of outbreaks/recurrences may reduce over time.

TargetRLF1: Syphilis develops in stages. The symptoms vary with each stage. But the stages may overlap. And the symptoms don't always happen in the same order. You may be infected with syphilis bacteria without noticing any symptoms for years. Primary syphilis: The first symptom of syphilis is a small sore called a chancre (SHANG-kur) that appears 2-12 weeks after exposure to someone with Syphilis. The sore is often painless. It appears at the spot where the bacteria entered your body. Most people with syphilis develop only one chancre. Some people get more than one. The chancre often forms about three weeks after you come in contact with syphilis bacteria. Many people who have syphilis don't notice the chancre. That's because it's usually painless. It also may be hidden within the vagina or rectum. The chancre heals on its own within 3 to 6 weeks. Secondary syphilis: While the chancre heals or a few weeks after it heals a Syphilis rash may develop; often unitchy, may appear rough, red, or reddish-brown and may be faint. It usually starts on the body's trunk, including chest, stomach, pelvis, back, and limbs. In time, it also could appear on the limbs, the palms of the hands and the soles of the feet. Besides the rash, other symptoms may include wartlike sores, hair loss, muscle aches, fever, sore throat, and fatigue. Symptoms of secondary syphilis may go away on their own. But without treatment, they could come and go for months or years. Latent syphilis: If you aren't treated for syphilis, the disease moves from the secondary stage to the latent stage. This also is called the hidden stage because you have no symptoms. The latent stage can last for years. Your symptoms may never come back. But without treatment, the disease might lead to major health problems, also called complications. Tertiary syphilis: After the latent stage, up to 30% to 40% of people with syphilis who don't get treatment have complications known as tertiary syphilis. Here, they may develop permanently damaged heart, brain, muscles, bones, and eyes. Congenital syphilis: Pregnant people who have syphilis can pass the disease to their babies. Unborn babies can become infected through the organ that provides nutrients and oxygen in the womb, called the placenta. Infection also can happen during birth. Newborns with congenital syphilis might have no symptoms. But without fast treatment, some babies might get sores and rashes on the skin, fever, a type of discolored skin and eyes called jaundice, not enough red blood cells (anemia), swollen spleen and liver, sneezing or a stuffed, drippy nose called rhinitis, bone changes, weight loss, and swollen lymph nodes. Later symptoms may include deafness, teeth problems, and saddle nose, a condition in which the bridge of the nose collapses. Babies with syphilis also can be born too early. They may die in the womb before birth, or they could die after birth.

TargetRLF1: A chlamydia also known as Chlamydial Genitourinary infection test detects the bacteria that cause chlamydia, a sexually transmitted infection (STI). This test tells you if you have the chlamydia infection so that you can get treat treatment and avoid complications. Or they may use a cell culture to see how chlamydia treatments are working. Because of the possibility of multiple sexually transmitted infections, all patients with any sexually transmitted disease (STD) should be evaluated for chlamydial infection. There are no risks involved with these tests. Rarely the results of the tests may be inconclusive or unclear and you may need to give another sample.

Blood tests do not actually detect the virus but look for antibodies.

If you have signs or symptoms of genital herpes at delivery, a 'C-section' is likely to occur.

TargetRLF1: While some people with Genital Herpes or Herpes Simplex Virus (HSV), also known as herpes will never have any symptoms, other people can develop symptoms within a few weeks of being infected. Common oral herpes symptoms include blisters (cold sores) or open sores (ulcers) in or around the mouth or lips. Most people notice a group or cluster of blisters or ulcers (lesions). These lesions burn and can be painful. They can appear on the buttocks, anus or thighs, on the vulva or vagina in women, and on the penis or scrotum in men. Often, before the lesions appear, patients describe a prodrome, characterized by a tingling or burning sensation in the area where the lesions will develop that can be noticed during urination, along with itching or discomfort in the genital area. You can also have the following symptoms, Blisters on the mouth or lips, Fever, headache or pain in the joints, Trouble urinating. In case of Neonatal Herpes, signs that your baby may have herpes are:irritability, blisters anywhere on her body, trouble breathing, grunting, blue appearance (cyanosis), rapid breathing, short periods of no breathing, jaundice, bleeding easily. People can have repeated outbreaks over time (‘recurrences’). These are usually shorter and less severe than the first outbreak. Herpes is a lifelong sexually transmitted infection, that cannot be cured. However, the number of outbreaks/recurrences may reduce over time.

TargetRLF1: A chlamydia also known as Chlamydial Genitourinary infection test detects the bacteria that cause chlamydia, a sexually transmitted infection (STI). This test tells you if you have the chlamydia infection so that you can get treat treatment and avoid complications.. Your provider takes a sample of urine or secretions from your vagina, penis or rectum and sends it to a lab for testing using a test called NAATs (short for nucleic acid amplification tests), which is very accurate and easy to take. Results are usually ready in a day. Less often, providers use a cell culture to test for chlamydia. In this case, your provider swabs your vagina, urethra or anus to collect a sample of fluid and cells. They send the cells to a lab to test. If bacteria are present, they will grow, which indicates an infection. Providers may choose this type of chlamydia test to detect infections in the anus. Or they may use a cell culture to see how chlamydia treatments are working. Your need for testing depends on your personal risk for getting Chlamydia. There are no risks involved with these tests. Rarely the results of the tests may be inconclusive or unclear and you may need to give another sample. You should get tested regularly if you have unprotected sex with a new partner, multiple partners or a partner who has an STI. You should also get tested if you have symptoms or you are pregnant. Many people with Chlamydia don't have symptoms. Because of the possibility of multiple sexually transmitted infections, all patients with any sexually transmitted disease (STD) should be evaluated for chlamydial infection.

TargetRLF1: Herpes can only be diagnosed at a health centre. You cannot test for it at home or using radiological methods. When a person has active herpes lesions (a.k.a. blisters, sores, ulcers), your healthcare provider may diagnose genital herpes by simply looking at any sores that are present, or a swab can be taken and tests done that can detect the virus directly. Blood tests do not actually detect the virus but look for antibodies.

To date, the earliest known case of HIV-1 infection in human blood is from a sample taken in 1959 from a man who died in Kinshasa in what was then the Belgian Congo. SIV probably entered the human population as a result of hunting chimpanzees. It is plausible that transmission could have occurred through a hunter being wounded and blood from a chimpanzee entering his bloodstream.  The origin of the Human Immunodeficiency Virus (HIV) has been a subject of scientific research and debate since the virus was identified in the 1980s.

TargetRLF1: A chlamydia also known as Chlamydial Genitourinary infection test detects the bacteria that cause chlamydia, a sexually transmitted infection (STI). This test tells you if you have the chlamydia infection so that you can get treat treatment and avoid complications. Your provider takes a sample of urine or secretions from your vagina, penis or rectum and sends it to a lab for testing using a test called NAATs (short for nucleic acid amplification tests), which is very accurate and easy to take. Results are usually ready in a day. Less often, providers use a cell culture to test for chlamydia. In this case, your provider swabs your vagina, urethra or anus to collect a sample of fluid and cells. They send the cells to a lab to test. If bacteria are present, they will grow, which indicates an infection. Providers may choose this type of chlamydia test to detect infections in the anus. Or they may use a cell culture to see how chlamydia treatments are working. Because of the possibility of multiple sexually transmitted infections, all patients with any sexually transmitted disease (STD) should be evaluated for chlamydial infection. There are no risks involved with these tests. Rarely the results of the tests may be inconclusive or unclear and you may need to give another sample.

TargetRLF1: People with symptoms of oral Genital herpes or Herpes Simplex Virus (HSV), also known as Herpes should avoid oral contact with others (including oral sex) and sharing objects that touched saliva. Individuals with symptoms of Genital Herpes or Herpes Simplex Virus (HSV), also known as herpes should abstain from sexual activity while experiencing symptoms. Both HSV-1 and HSV-2 are most contagious when sores are present but can also be transmitted when no symptoms are felt or visible. For sexually active people, consistent and correct use of condoms is the best way to prevent genital herpes and other STIs. Condoms reduce the risk; however, HSV infection can still occur through contact with genital or anal areas not covered by the condom. Medical male circumcision can provide life-long partial protection against HSV-2 infection, as well as against HIV and human papillomavirus (HPV). Pregnant women with symptoms of genital herpes should inform their health care providers. Preventing acquisition of HSV-2 infection is particularly important for women in late pregnancy when the risk for neonatal herpes is greatest.

TargetRLF1: There are several hormones involved in puberty, each with specific roles:  Estrogen: This hormone is responsible for breast development in girls, widening of the hips, and other female secondary sexual characteristics. Testosterone: This hormone is responsible for the deepening of the voice, growth of facial and body hair, muscle development, and other male secondary sexual characteristics.  Growth Hormone: As the name suggests, growth hormone is responsible for growth spurts during puberty. It stimulates the growth of bones, muscles, and organs.  Adrenal Hormones: Hormones produced by the adrenal glands, such as cortisol and DHEA, also increase during puberty. These hormones can affect mood, energy levels, and how the body responds to stress.  These hormones work together to orchestrate the changes happening in your body during puberty. While these changes can feel overwhelming at times, they're all part of the amazing process of growing up.

TargetRLF1: Syphilis is treatable and curable. People who suspect they may have syphilis should speak to their healthcare provider. The early stage of syphilis is treated with a benzathine penicillin (BPG) injection. BPG is the first line treatment for syphilis and the only WHO-recommended treatment for pregnant women with syphilis. As second line treatment, doctors may also use doxycycline, ceftriaxone or azithromycin, which are antibiotic medicines is also used to treat later stages of syphilis, but more doses are required. Doses are usually given once per week for three weeks, including when it is not possible to identify the stage of infection. Your partner should also get treatment. Do not have sex (vaginal, anal or oral) until you and your partner have finished treatment and tests have shown treatment has worked. BPG can prevent syphilis from being passed from a mother to baby. Babies born with syphilis (congenital syphilis), or babies whose mother had untreated syphilis, need to be treated right away to avoid serious health problems. Aqueous benzyl penicillin or procaine penicillin is recommended in infants with confirmed congenital syphilis or infants who are clinically healthy but whose mothers had untreated syphilis, inadequately treated syphilis (including treatment within 30 days of delivery), or syphilis treated with non-penicillin regimens. Unfortunately, while Syphilis can be cured, there is no way to repair organs damaged by syphilis.
